lesson.title: Where the Curve Touches Home: Finding and Reading Intercepts
lesson.summary: Intercepts anchor a curve to the axes, and the multiplicity of each root reveals whether the graph crosses straight through the x-axis or just grazes it and bounces back.
lesson.body:
Finding intercepts is usually the easiest step of curve sketching mechanically, plug in x = 0 for the y-intercept and set the function equal to zero for the x-intercepts, but reading what each root means for the shape of the graph takes a bit more care, especially for factors that repeat.

Let f(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)^2, already conveniently factored. The y-intercept is f(0) = (2)(1)^2 = 2, so the graph passes through (0, 2). The x-intercepts come from setting each factor to zero: x = -2 (from the factor x + 2, appearing to the first power) and x = 1 (from the factor (x - 1)^2, appearing to the second power).

Those two roots behave completely differently on the graph, and the difference is entirely about multiplicity, how many times each factor repeats. At x = -2, the multiplicity is 1, an odd number, and odd-multiplicity roots always produce a genuine crossing: check the sign of f just to either side. For x slightly less than -2, (x + 2) is negative and (x - 1)^2 is positive, so f is negative; for x slightly greater than -2, (x + 2) is positive and (x - 1)^2 is still positive, so f is positive. The sign flips from negative to positive, confirming the curve crosses the x-axis there, heading upward.

At x = 1, the multiplicity is 2, an even number, and even-multiplicity roots never produce a crossing; instead the curve touches the axis and bounces back the way it came. Check the sign near x = 1: (x - 1)^2 is nonnegative everywhere, equaling exactly zero only at x = 1 itself, and (x + 2) is close to 3 (positive) throughout this neighborhood. So f(x) is approximately 3(x - 1)^2 near x = 1, which is greater than or equal to zero on both sides. The curve touches the x-axis at x = 1 and immediately rises back above it on both sides, the signature of an even-multiplicity root. In general, odd multiplicity means cross, even multiplicity means touch and bounce, and this pattern generalizes to any multiplicity: multiplicity 3 crosses but flattens against the axis as it does, multiplicity 4 touches and bounces but flattens more than multiplicity 2 does, and so on.

Two more situations round out intercept analysis. Some functions have no x-intercepts at all: f(x) = x^2 + 1 is always positive, since x^2 ≥ 0 for every real x, so x^2 + 1 ≥ 1 > 0 everywhere, and the graph never touches the x-axis. And for rational functions, an x-intercept must come from a zero of the numerator that survives after checking the domain; a numerator zero that coincides with a denominator zero is not an intercept at all, it is a hole, since the function is not even defined there. This is the same distinction that came up in domain analysis: always find the domain before trusting a root of the numerator as a genuine intercept.
